text_blocks.snippet: The primary symptoms of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) result from high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which forces the right side of the heart to work harder and reduces oxygen flow.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Often the first and most prominent sign, initially occurring during physical exertion (such as climbing stairs or walking) and worsening over time to happen even at rest.
Fatigue and weakness: Persistent tiredness and reduced exercise capacity due to the heart struggling to deliver enough oxygenated blood to the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Discomfort, angina-like pain, or tightness caused by an overworked and strained right heart ventricle.
Dizziness and lightheadedness: Occurs frequently during or after physical activity because of reduced blood flow and oxygen to the brain.
Heart palpitations: A fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat as the heart tries to compensate for the high pressure.

text_blocks.snippet: As the condition advances and right-sided heart strain or failure develops, more severe signs appear:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema): Fluid retention leading to swollen ankles, legs, feet, or a bloated/distended abdomen (ascites).
Fainting spells (syncope): Episodes of fainting, particularly during or right after exertion, as blood pressure or oxygen drops sharply.
Cyanosis: A bluish tint to the lips, skin, or fingers caused by low oxygen levels in the blood.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis): A rare but serious complication resulting from high pressure in the small blood vessels of the lungs.
Hoarseness: Can occur if an enlarged pulmonary artery presses on the nerves in the chest.

text_blocks.snippet: Learn more about managing the condition through the American Lung Association or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
